people.name: Constantine the Great
people.short_bio: First Christian Roman emperor. Issued the Edict of Milan (313), convened the Council of Nicaea (325), and was baptized on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia.

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.short_bio: Father of Church History. Bishop of Caesarea, biographer of Constantine, and author of the Ecclesiastical History, the chief source for the first three centuries of Christianity.

people.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
people.short_bio: Bishop of Alexandria and chief defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. Five times exiled. Wrote On the Incarnation and the Vita Antonii.

people.name: Arius
people.short_bio: Alexandrian presbyter whose teaching that the Son was a created being sparked the Arian controversy. Condemned at Nicaea (325). Heretic.

people.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
people.short_bio: Bishop of Nicomedia, then of Constantinople. Leader of the Arian party at and after Nicaea. Baptized Constantine on his deathbed.

people.name: Hilary of Poitiers
people.short_bio: Bishop of Poitiers and 'Athanasius of the West.' Defender of Nicene Trinitarianism in Latin; wrote De Trinitate while exiled in Phrygia.

people.name: Marius Victorinus
people.short_bio: African rhetorician at Rome, Neoplatonist, who converted to Christianity in old age. Wrote anti-Arian Trinitarian treatises and a famous influence on Augustine.

people.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
people.short_bio: Bishop of Jerusalem. His Catechetical Lectures are a primary witness to fourth-century baptismal preparation and liturgy.

people.name: Ephrem the Syrian
people.short_bio: Syriac deacon, hymnographer and poet-theologian of Nisibis and Edessa. Author of the Hymns on Faith and Hymns on Paradise.

people.name: Aphrahat
people.short_bio: Persian Christian sage who wrote 23 Demonstrations in Syriac (337-345), among the earliest surviving Syriac Christian theological works.

people.name: Basil of Caesarea
people.short_bio: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, founder of cenobitic monastic rules in the East, author of On the Holy Spirit. One of the three Cappadocian Fathers.

citations.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oratio 43 (Funeral oration on Basil)

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.short_bio: Cappadocian Father, briefly Archbishop of Constantinople (380-381) and presider over the First Council of Constantinople. Known as 'the Theologian' for his Five Theological Orations.

citations.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, De Vita Sua

people.name: Gregory of Nyssa
people.short_bio: Younger brother of Basil and the third Cappadocian Father. Author of the Life of Moses, Catechetical Oration, and Life of Macrina.

people.name: Macrina the Younger
people.short_bio: Eldest sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa. Ascetic teacher who established a monastic community on the family estate at Annisa; subject of Gregory of Nyssa's Vita.

citations.source: Gregory of Nyssa, De Anima et Resurrectione

people.name: Peter of Sebaste
people.short_bio: Youngest brother of Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina. Bishop of Sebaste from c. 380.

people.name: Didymus the Blind
people.short_bio: Blind from childhood; head of the Alexandrian catechetical school. Wrote on the Holy Spirit and on the Trinity. Posthumously condemned for Origenism.

people.name: Evagrius Ponticus
people.short_bio: Pontic monk in the Egyptian desert. Pioneer of systematic monastic theology (Praktikos, Chapters on Prayer); originated the eight 'logismoi' that became the seven deadly sins.

people.name: John Cassian
people.short_bio: Brought Egyptian monastic spirituality to the Latin West. Author of the Institutes and Conferences; founded monasteries at Marseilles.

people.name: Anthony the Great
people.short_bio: Father of Christian monasticism. Egyptian hermit whose Vita by Athanasius shaped Christian asceticism East and West.

people.name: Pachomius the Great
people.short_bio: Founder of cenobitic (communal) monasticism in Egypt. Established the monastery at Tabennisi and wrote the first monastic rule.

people.name: Macarius the Great
people.short_bio: Egyptian desert father, founder of the monastic settlement of Scetis. Subject of many sayings in the Apophthegmata Patrum.

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.short_bio: Archbishop of Constantinople, called 'Golden-Mouth' for his preaching. Greatest preacher of the Greek Fathers; deposed and exiled at the Synod of the Oak (403).

citations.source: Palladius, Dialogus de Vita Joannis Chrysostomi

people.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
people.short_bio: Bishop of Mopsuestia, leading Antiochene exegete and teacher of Nestorius. Posthumously condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople (553).

people.name: Diodore of Tarsus
people.short_bio: Bishop of Tarsus, founder of the Antiochene exegetical school in its mature form. Teacher of John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

people.name: Ambrose of Milan
people.short_bio: Bishop of Milan and one of the four Latin Doctors. Confronted emperors Theodosius and Valentinian; baptized Augustine in 387.

people.name: Jerome
people.short_bio: Translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible; biblical scholar and prolific letter-writer. Settled in Bethlehem from 386.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.short_bio: Bishop of Hippo and the most influential Latin Father. Author of Confessions, City of God, On the Trinity, and the anti-Pelagian works.

people.name: Alypius of Thagaste
people.short_bio: Lifelong friend of Augustine, with whom he was baptized by Ambrose in 387. Bishop of Thagaste from 394.

people.name: Possidius of Calama
people.short_bio: Bishop of Calama and disciple of Augustine. Wrote the Vita Augustini and compiled an Indiculus of Augustine's works.

people.name: Monica
people.short_bio: Mother of Augustine of Hippo. Devout Christian whose persistent prayers Augustine credits with his conversion.

people.name: Pelagius
people.short_bio: British ascetic teacher at Rome whose denial of original sin and emphasis on free will sparked the Pelagian controversy. Condemned at Carthage (418) and Ephesus (431). Heretic.

people.name: Caelestius
people.short_bio: Disciple and chief associate of Pelagius. Condemned at Carthage (411 and 418).

citations.source: Augustine, De Gratia Christi et de Peccato Originali

people.name: Julian of Eclanum
people.short_bio: Bishop of Eclanum, intellectually most formidable Pelagian theologian. Deposed for refusing to sign the Tractoria of Pope Zosimus; opposed by Augustine in Contra Julianum.

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.short_bio: Patriarch of Alexandria. Chief architect of Christological orthodoxy; presided over the Council of Ephesus (431) which condemned Nestorius.

people.name: Nestorius
people.short_bio: Archbishop of Constantinople (428-431). Condemned at Ephesus (431) for distinguishing two persons in Christ and denying the title Theotokos. Heretic.

people.name: Theodoret of Cyrus
people.short_bio: Bishop of Cyrrhus, Antiochene exegete and historian. Author of an Ecclesiastical History; defended Nestorius then accepted Chalcedon (451).

people.name: Pope Damasus I
people.short_bio: Bishop of Rome 366-384. Patron of Jerome who commissioned the Vulgate. Established the canon of Scripture at the Roman Synod (382).

people.name: Pope Innocent I
people.short_bio: Bishop of Rome 401-417. Defended John Chrysostom and confirmed the African councils' condemnation of Pelagianism (417).

people.name: Pope Celestine I
people.short_bio: Bishop of Rome 422-432. Backed Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius and sent legates to Ephesus (431); reportedly sent Palladius to Ireland (431).

people.name: Pope Leo I
people.short_bio: Bishop of Rome 440-461. His Tome (Epistula 28) was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon (451). Negotiated with Attila in 452.

people.name: Vincent of Lérins
people.short_bio: Monk of Lérins. Author of the Commonitorium, which formulated the canon of catholic tradition: 'what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.'

people.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
people.short_bio: Lay theologian and chronicler. Disciple and defender of Augustine against semi-Pelagians; corresponded with him; continued Jerome's Chronicon.

people.name: Sulpicius Severus
people.short_bio: Aquitanian aristocrat turned ascetic. Wrote the Vita Martini (life of Martin of Tours) and a Chronicle covering biblical and church history to 400.

people.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
people.short_bio: Latin translator and historian. Translated Origen, Eusebius (continuing the HE to 395), and the Sentences of Sextus. Friend turned bitter opponent of Jerome over Origenism.

people.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
people.short_bio: Bishop of Salamis on Cyprus. Heresiologist; author of the Panarion ('Medicine Chest') against 80 heresies. Vigorous opponent of Origenism.

people.name: Paulinus of Nola
people.short_bio: Aquitanian aristocrat and poet who renounced wealth for asceticism. Bishop of Nola from c. 409. Correspondent of Augustine, Jerome, Sulpicius Severus, and Ambrose.

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.short_bio: Apostle and patron saint of Armenia. Converted King Tiridates III, leading to Armenia's adoption of Christianity (c. 301).

people.name: Mesrop Mashtots
people.short_bio: Inventor of the Armenian alphabet (c. 405) and translator of the Bible into Armenian. Also credited with Georgian and Caucasian Albanian scripts.

people.name: Patrick of Ireland
people.short_bio: British missionary bishop who evangelized Ireland in the fifth century. Wrote the Confessio and the Letter to Coroticus, the only sure primary documents.

people.name: Alexander of Alexandria
people.short_bio: Patriarch of Alexandria 313-326. First to condemn Arius locally (c. 318); led the orthodox party at Nicaea; mentor of Athanasius.

people.name: Marcellus of Ancyra
people.short_bio: Bishop of Ancyra. Strong anti-Arian at Nicaea but accused of Sabellianism. Friend of Athanasius; suspected by the Eusebian party.

people.name: Martin of Tours
people.short_bio: Soldier turned monk and bishop of Tours. Pioneer of Western monasticism; subject of Sulpicius Severus's Vita Martini.

people.name: Socrates Scholasticus
people.short_bio: Lay historian. His Ecclesiastical History (305-439) continues Eusebius and is a primary source for the fourth and early fifth centuries.

citations.source: Socrates Scholasticus, Hist. Eccl. (preface and passim)

people.name: Sozomen
people.short_bio: Lawyer at Constantinople and ecclesiastical historian. His HE covers 323-425, paralleling Socrates Scholasticus.

people.name: Palladius of Galatia
people.short_bio: Disciple of Evagrius Ponticus and bishop of Helenopolis. Author of the Lausiac History on Egyptian monasticism and the Dialogue on the life of John Chrysostom.

citations.source: Palladius, Dialogus de Vita Joannis Chrysostomi

people.name: Gregory the Elder of Nazianzus
people.short_bio: Bishop of Nazianzus and father of Gregory the Theologian. Converted from the Hypsistarii sect; ordained his son presbyter.

citations.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oratio 18 (funeral oration on his father)

people.name: Amphilochius of Iconium
people.short_bio: Cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus and close friend of Basil. Bishop of Iconium; sometimes counted among the Cappadocians.

people.name: Flavian of Constantinople
people.short_bio: Archbishop of Constantinople 446-449. Recipient of Leo's Tome; condemned Eutyches at the Home Synod (448); deposed and beaten at the 'Robber Council' of Ephesus (449).

people.name: Eutyches
people.short_bio: Archimandrite at Constantinople whose monophysite teaching ('one nature after the union') was condemned at the Home Synod (448) and at Chalcedon (451). Heretic.

people.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
people.short_bio: Patriarch of Alexandria 444-451. Successor of Cyril; presided over the 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus (449); deposed at Chalcedon (451).

people.name: Chromatius of Aquileia
people.short_bio: Bishop of Aquileia from 388. Patron of both Jerome and Rufinus; commissioned biblical translations and exegetical works.

people.name: Helena
people.short_bio: Mother of Constantine the Great. Pilgrim to the Holy Land (c. 326-328); traditionally credited with discovering the True Cross and founding churches at Bethlehem and the Mount of Olives.

relationships.notes: Eusebius preserves multiple letters from Constantine and delivered an oration in his presence.
Eusebius wrote the Vita Constantini and the Tricennial Oration in his honour.
Constantine received baptism from Eusebius of Nicomedia on his deathbed in 337.
Helena was the mother of Constantine.
Athanasius served as deacon and secretary to Alexander, accompanying him to Nicaea.
Athanasius succeeded Alexander as bishop of Alexandria in 328.
Alexander first condemned Arius and excommunicated him c. 318.
Athanasius's life work was the refutation of Arianism.
Eusebius of Nicomedia was Arius's chief patron and protector after his condemnation.
Athanasius wrote the Vita Antonii and reports having served Anthony personally.
Anthony visited Alexandria in support of Athanasius against the Arians (338).
Macrina spiritually shaped her younger brother Basil after his return from Athens.
Gregory portrays Macrina as his teacher in De Anima et Resurrectione.

citations.source: Gregory of Nyssa, De Anima et Resurrectione (preface)

relationships.notes: Gregory describes Basil as his teacher and elder brother.
Macrina raised the youngest brother Peter herself.
Basil and Gregory were close friends from their student days at Athens.
Surviving correspondence and the joint Philocalia of Origen.
Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled the Philocalia, an anthology of Origen.
Co-compiler with Basil of the Philocalia of Origen.
Basil's De Spiritu Sancto is dedicated to Amphilochius.
Amphilochius was a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus.
Gregory the Theologian was raised and ordained presbyter by his father.

citations.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, De Vita Sua

relationships.notes: Gregory ordained Evagrius deacon and trained him at Constantinople.
Evagrius sat at the feet of Macarius the Great and Macarius the Alexandrian in the desert (Palladius, contemporary).
Cassian's Conferences transmit Evagrian monastic doctrine, though Cassian never names him.
Cassian was ordained deacon by Chrysostom and travelled to Rome to plead his cause.
Pachomius is depicted as familiar with the Antonian model though they did not directly meet.
Chrysostom was a pupil of Diodore at Antioch.
Theodore studied alongside Chrysostom under Diodore.
Nestorius is traditionally counted as a pupil of Theodore at Antioch.
Theodoret defended Theodore's writings.
Ambrose baptized Augustine and Alypius at Milan during the Easter Vigil of 387.
Augustine attended Ambrose's preaching at Milan and credits him with his conversion.
Baptized together with Augustine in 387.
Augustine credits his mother Monica with persistent influence toward his conversion.
Lifelong friendship from Thagaste through Carthage, Rome, Milan and back to Africa.
Possidius lived in Augustine's monastic community at Hippo and wrote his Vita.
Augustine was deeply moved by hearing of the conversion of Marius Victorinus.
Extensive (often acrimonious) correspondence over Galatians and the Hebrew text of the OT.
Friends from youth in Aquileia who became bitter opponents over Origenism.
The Origenist controversy split the two former friends c. 393-402.
Damasus commissioned Jerome's revision of the Latin Bible.
Jerome and Epiphanius were close allies in the Origenist controversy.
Rufinus translated Origen's De Principiis and many homilies into Latin.
Rufinus translated and continued Eusebius's HE.
The Pelagian controversy occupied Augustine's last two decades.
Augustine wrote six books Contra Julianum and the unfinished Opus Imperfectum.
Augustine wrote against Caelestius alongside Pelagius.

citations.source: Augustine, De Gratia Christi et de Peccato Originali

relationships.notes: Caelestius was Pelagius's chief disciple and propagator.
Jerome wrote a Dialogus contra Pelagianos.
Cyril led the condemnation of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431).
Theodoret wrote a refutation of Cyril's Twelve Anathemas.
Celestine commissioned Cyril to act on his behalf against Nestorius.

citations.source: Acta Concilii Ephesini (431); letters of Celestine to Cyril

relationships.notes: Leo's Tome (Ep. 28) was addressed to Flavian.
Flavian condemned Eutyches at the Home Synod of 448.
Leo condemned Eutyches's monophysitism in his Tome.
Dioscorus succeeded Cyril as patriarch of Alexandria in 444.
Dioscorus presided over Flavian's deposition at the Robber Council of Ephesus (449).
Cyril repeatedly invokes Athanasius as the standard of orthodoxy.
Ambrose's De Spiritu Sancto draws heavily on Basil; correspondence between Eastern and Western Nicenes.
Ambrose's De Spiritu Sancto adapts Basil's work of the same title.
Lengthy correspondence preserved on both sides.
Paulinus exchanged letters with Jerome on biblical study.
Ambrose ordained Paulinus presbyter at Nola.
Lifelong correspondence between fellow Aquitanian aristocrat-ascetics.
Sulpicius personally visited Martin and wrote his Vita.

Hilary received Martin and ordained him exorcist; Martin founded Ligugé under Hilary's patronage. Sole source is Sulpicius Severus' Vita Martini, a hagiography written ~397 with strong panegyric framing.
Prosper consulted Augustine on the rise of semi-Pelagianism in southern Gaul.
Prosper systematically defended Augustine's doctrine of grace.

citations.source: Prosper, Pro Augustino Responsiones; Contra Collatorem

relationships.notes: Prosper's Contra Collatorem refutes Cassian's Conference 13.
Vincent's Commonitorium is widely (though disputedly) read as a critique of Augustinian predestinarianism.
Didymus's exegesis is heavily Origenist; he was condemned with Origen at Constantinople II (553).
Jerome studied with Didymus at Alexandria c. 386.
Rufinus also studied under Didymus at Alexandria.
Epiphanius led the late-fourth-century campaign against Origenism.
Chrysostom and Epiphanius clashed over Origenism at Constantinople in 403.
Palladius lived with Evagrius for nine years in the desert.
Palladius wrote the Dialogus on Chrysostom's life.

citations.source: Palladius, Dialogus de Vita Joannis Chrysostomi

relationships.notes: Socrates' Hist. Eccl. begins where Eusebius left off.
Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates.
Theodoret continues Eusebius in his Hist. Eccl.
Mesrop worked under the catholicate descended from Gregory's line; tradition links them.
Patrick's mission is traditionally connected to Celestine's earlier sending of Palladius.
Chromatius supported Jerome's biblical work financially and by patronage.
Chromatius was Rufinus's bishop and friend.

Leo became Bishop of Rome (440) following Sixtus III, who succeeded Celestine. Not a direct succession; relationship compresses an intervening pontificate. Source is the Liber Pontificalis, redacted in the 6th c.
Celestine became Bishop of Rome (422) following Boniface, who succeeded Zosimus, who succeeded Innocent — not a direct succession. Source is the Liber Pontificalis, redacted in the 6th c.
Innocent became Bishop of Rome (401) following Anastasius, Siricius, and Damasus — three intervening bishops. Source is the Liber Pontificalis.
Chrysostom appealed to Innocent after his deposition.
Nestorius became Archbishop of Constantinople (428) some years after Chrysostom (d. 407), via intervening bishops Arsacius, Atticus, and Sisinnius — not a direct succession.
Flavian became Archbishop of Constantinople (446) several bishops after Nestorius (Maximian, Proclus); not a direct succession.
Cyril became Patriarch of Alexandria (412) several bishops after Athanasius (d. 373) — Peter II, Timothy, Theophilus all intervened. Not a direct succession.
Marcellus and Athanasius were exiled to Rome together c. 339-343.
Eusebius wrote Contra Marcellum and De Ecclesiastica Theologia against him.
Ambrose received Monica's commendation regarding Augustine.
Hilary cited Athanasius and the Nicene cause; took up Athanasius's role in the West.
Basil wrote to Athanasius seeking unity with Rome.
Basil ordained Evagrius lector at Caesarea.
Late tradition reports a visit between Ephrem and Basil at Caesarea.
Cyril sent Augustine documents on the Nestorian controversy shortly before Augustine's death.
Both attended the First Council of Constantinople in 381; Cyril is listed among the 150 fathers and Gregory presided briefly over the council.

citations.source: Acta of the First Council of Constantinople (381)

relationships.notes: Cyril's Catechetical Lectures defend the Nicene faith and oppose Arian subordinationism, and he subscribed the Nicene-Constantinopolitan creed at the council of 381.

Ephrem and Aphrahat are the two principal 4th-century Syriac Fathers and share the same theological idiom (typological exegesis, anti-Jewish polemic, ascetic ideals). Direct citation is not preserved; the link is the shared Syriac milieu and parallel content noted by modern scholarship.

citations.source: Murray, Symbols of Church and Kingdom (CUP 1975), pp. 29-38

relationships.notes: Agathangelos's History of the Armenians records a journey of King Trdat and Gregory to Rome to meet Constantine; the historicity is debated but the tradition links them as contemporary Christian rulers/founders.
The 5th-century Armenian translation school founded by Mesrop and Sahak rendered Chrysostom's homilies into Armenian; Koriun describes the translation programme.

citations.source: Thomson, A Bibliography of Classical Armenian Literature to 1500 AD (Brepols 1995), s.v. John Chrysostom
